question: Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) act primarily by preventing ovulation or fertilisation, and do NOT act as abortifacients — making them legal and ethically permissible under India's Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. ECPs work by delaying ovulation — they do not terminate an established pregnancy and are not governed by the MTP Act. This misconception is one of the most common barriers to ECP uptake in community practice, making it critical to address in counselling.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. ECPs (levonorgestrel-based) primarily delay or inhibit ovulation; the post-fertilisation effect, if any, is unproven at pharmacological doses used. They are neither classified as abortifacients nor regulated under the MTP Act. Counselling must address this misconception to improve uptake.
